claim: Autoimmune Polyglandular syndrome type 1 (APS1) is caused by monogenic mutations in the AIRE gene.
source: Autoimmune Polyglandular syndrome type 1 (APS1) or Autoimmune Polyglandular-Candidiasis-Ectodermal Dystrophy (APECED; OMIM #240300) is an autoimmune syndrome caused by monogenic mutations in the AIRE gene that result in defects in AIRE-dependent T cell education in the thymus (Aaltonen et al., 1997; Anderson et al., 2002; Conteduca et al., 2018; Malchow et al., 2016; Nagamine et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is directly stated in the text and supported by multiple citations to published literature.

claim: AIRE gene mutations result in defects in AIRE-dependent T cell education in the thymus.
source: Autoimmune Polyglandular syndrome type 1 (APS1) or Autoimmune Polyglandular-Candidiasis-Ectodermal Dystrophy (APECED; OMIM #240300) is an autoimmune syndrome caused by monogenic mutations in the AIRE gene that result in defects in AIRE-dependent T cell education in the thymus (Aaltonen et al., 1997; Anderson et al., 2002; Conteduca et al., 2018; Malchow et al., 2016; Nagamine et al., 1997).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to published research.

claim: People with APS1 develop autoimmunity to multiple organs, including endocrine organs, skin, gut, and lung.
source: As a result, people with APS1 develop autoimmunity to multiple organs, including endocrine organs, skin, gut, and lung (Ahonen et al., 1990; Ferre et al., 2016; Söderbergh et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to published studies.

claim: The majority of APS1 autoimmune manifestations are thought to be primarily driven by autoreactive T cells.
source: Although the majority of APS1 autoimmune manifestations are thought to be primarily driven by autoreactive T cells, people with APS1 also possess autoreactive B cells and corresponding high-affinity autoantibody responses (Devoss et al., 2008; Gavanescu et al., 2008; Meyer et al., 2016; Sng et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to published research.

claim: People with APS1 possess autoreactive B cells and corresponding high-affinity autoantibody responses.
source: Although the majority of APS1 autoimmune manifestations are thought to be primarily driven by autoreactive T cells, people with APS1 also possess autoreactive B cells and corresponding high-affinity autoantibody responses (Devoss et al., 2008; Gavanescu et al., 2008; Meyer et al., 2016; Sng et al., 2019).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to published research.

claim: Autoantibodies in APS1 likely derive from germinal center reactions driven by self-reactive T cells.
source: These autoantibodies likely derive from germinal center reactions driven by self-reactive T cells, resulting in mirroring of autoantigen identities between the T and B cell compartments (Lanzavecchia, 1985; Meyer et al., 2016).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to published research.

claim: GAD65 was identified as a major autoantigen in type 1 diabetes by using sera from people with Stiff Person Syndrome.
source: Indeed, such an approach identified GAD65 as a major autoantigen in type 1 diabetes by using sera from people with Stiff Person Syndrome (OMIM #184850), who harbor high affinity autoantibodies (Baekkeskov et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: People with Stiff Person Syndrome harbor high affinity autoantibodies.
source: Indeed, such an approach identified GAD65 as a major autoantigen in type 1 diabetes by using sera from people with Stiff Person Syndrome (OMIM #184850), who harbor high affinity autoantibodies (Baekkeskov et al., 1990).
evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by a citation to published research.

claim: BPIFB1 autoantibodies are used to assess people with APS1 for risk of interstitial lung disease.

evidence: The claim is directly stated and supported by citations to published research.

claim: BPIFB1 autoantibodies were discovered first in Aire-deficient mice using a combination of targeted immunoblotting, tissue microscopy, and mass spectrometry.

These data suggest that people with APS1 often target similar, but not identical protein regions.
